subtopic_detail: White atrophic vulval plaques with architectural change and the role of biopsy alongside treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman referred with two years of vulval itch that is worst at night. She has been given three courses of topical antifungal cream and a low potency hydrocortisone ointment by different doctors with no lasting benefit, and says intercourse has become painful at the entrance.

The labia minora are partly resorbed into the labia majora and the clitoral hood is fused over the clitoris. There are ivory white thickened plaques extending around the vulva and perianal skin in a figure of eight, with two small areas of purpura but no ulcer, nodule or fixed thickening. The vaginal mucosa itself is normal.

data_table.Examination: White sclerotic plaques over labia and perianal skin, loss of labia minora, clitoral hood fusion, purpura, no ulcer or nodule, normal vaginal epithelium
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab for candida negative; no biopsy performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a potent topical corticosteroid ointment with long term maintenance and review
options.rationale: An ultrapotent or potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for this sclerosing dermatosis, and continued maintenance rather than a short burst is what controls symptoms and reduces later scarring and malignancy (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Prescribe a further course of topical antifungal cream and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Repeating an antifungal after a negative swab and three failed courses treats the wrong diagnosis, and architectural loss is not a feature of candidal vulvitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly and review the vulval appearance in three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary atrophy of menopause, whose distinguishing feature is a pale thin vaginal mucosa rather than white plaques on keratinised vulval and perianal skin (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses).

options.text: Arrange a vulval punch biopsy first and withhold all treatment until the histology returns
options.rationale: Biopsy is mandatory for an ulcer, nodule, fixed thickening or failure to respond, but the appearance here is characteristic and withholding treatment leaves her symptomatic for weeks (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses).

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the fused clitoral hood and resurfacing of the vulval skin
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for the functional consequences of scarring or for proven malignancy, and operating on active inflamed skin risks recurrence at the incision (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses).

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis of the anogenital skin that classically produces intense nocturnal itch, ivory white sclerotic plaques in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus, purpura from fragile skin, and progressive architectural loss with resorption of the labia minora and burial of the clitoris. It is frequently mistaken for candidiasis or atrophy and treated with antifungals or oestrogen for years before the diagnosis is made. Treatment is a potent or ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, initially daily and then reduced to a maintenance frequency that is continued indefinitely, because ongoing control reduces both scarring and the risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Around 4 to 5 per cent of affected women develop that malignancy, so any ulcer, nodule, fixed area or lesion that fails to respond to adequate steroid must be biopsied.
key_points: Nocturnal itch with white plaques and loss of labia minora is the defining picture
The distribution is a figure of eight around vulva and anus with sparing of the vagina
Potent topical corticosteroid with long term maintenance is the standard treatment
Biopsy any ulcer, nodule, fixed thickening or steroid unresponsive area
Lifelong surveillance is needed because of the squamous cell carcinoma risk
explanation.pearls: Sparing of the vaginal mucosa separates lichen sclerosus from erosive lichen planus, which involves the vagina and can cause vaginal stenosis, and that single examination finding changes both treatment intensity and prognosis.

subtopic_detail: Imaging and first line treatment choice in heavy menstrual bleeding with a diffusely enlarged uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 42 year old woman describes eight years of increasingly heavy periods that now flood through a pad hourly on the worst two days, with deep cramping pain that starts three days before bleeding and continues throughout. Her family is complete and she does not want surgery if it can be avoided.

On examination the uterus is smoothly enlarged to about 12 weeks size, is tender on bimanual palpation and is mobile with no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globally bulky uterus with asymmetric myometrial thickening, indistinct border between endometrium and myometrium and small myometrial cysts, and no discrete mass. The endometrium is 6 mm and regular. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115-165) and her ferritin is 8 mcg/L (15-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Smoothly enlarged tender mobile uterus of about 12 weeks size, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound as described; endometrial thickness 6 mm; haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 mcg/L (15-200)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and start oral iron replacement at the same time
options.rationale: Embolisation is an established option for fibroids and is used selectively for diffuse myometrial disease, but it is not the first line treatment when a reversible medical option has not been tried (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Perform hysteroscopy with endometrial resection and start oral iron replacement afterwards
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation targets the endometrium, whereas the pathology here lies within the myometrium, so failure rates and later hysterectomy are high in this group (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device and treat the iron deficiency with oral iron
options.rationale: The ultrasound pattern of a bulky uterus with indistinct junctional zone and myometrial cysts indicates adenomyosis, for which a levonorgestrel intrauterine device is the first line uterus conserving treatment and also addresses the dysmenorrhoea (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange endometrial pipelle sampling and defer any treatment until the histology is available
options.rationale: Sampling is indicated for a thickened or irregular endometrium or for persistent bleeding after treatment failure, and a regular 6 mm endometrium in a premenopausal woman does not require it before starting therapy (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid on bleeding days only and review her haemoglobin in six months
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by around a third but does not treat the associated pain or the underlying myometrial disease, so it is a partial answer for a woman with this symptom burden (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding with a bulky uterus is commonly assumed to be fibroids, but adenomyosis produces a different ultrasound signature and responds to different treatment. The features that separate them are a globally enlarged tender uterus with asymmetric myometrial thickening, loss of a crisp junctional zone and small myometrial cysts, as against a discrete well demarcated mass with a peripheral vascular rim in a fibroid. The distinction matters because endometrial ablation performs poorly in adenomyosis, since the disease sits deep in the myometrium rather than at the surface. A levonorgestrel intrauterine device is the first line uterus conserving treatment because it addresses both the bleeding and the dysmenorrhoea, and correcting the iron deficiency is a necessary parallel step rather than an alternative.
key_points: A tender globally bulky uterus with an indistinct junctional zone suggests adenomyosis
A discrete demarcated myometrial mass with a peripheral rim suggests a fibroid
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device is first line for uterus conserving treatment
Endometrial ablation has high failure rates when the disease is myometrial
Always treat the coexisting iron deficiency, not just the bleeding
explanation.pearls: Magnetic resonance imaging showing a junctional zone thickness above 12 mm supports adenomyosis when the ultrasound is equivocal, and it is the investigation to request before committing a woman to hysterectomy.

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in a patient requesting a hypnotic
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 46 year old accountant has had trouble sleeping for eight months. He takes about 90 minutes to fall asleep, wakes at 3 am and lies awake for an hour or more, and this happens five or six nights a week. He is irritable and unproductive at work.

He has started going to bed at 8.30 pm to give himself the best chance, spends time in bed reading work emails, and naps for an hour most afternoons. He drinks two coffees before midday and no alcohol. He denies low mood, anhedonia, worry or panic, and he does not snore, has no restless sensations in his legs and his partner has seen no breathing pauses. His thyroid function and full blood count taken last week were normal. He asks directly for a script for zolpidem.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, Mallampati class 1 airway, normal mental state examination with euthymic mood and full affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits; Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 6 of 24

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe zolpidem nightly for four weeks with a plan to taper it after that period
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine receptor agonist gives short term benefit only, carries risks of tolerance, falls and complex sleep behaviours, and is reserved for brief use when non drug treatment is unavailable or has failed (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction and stimulus control
options.rationale: Structured behavioural therapy is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia disorder and directly targets the excessive time in bed, the daytime napping and the use of the bed for work that are perpetuating his pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Prescribe low dose amitriptyline at night and review the effect on his sleep in six weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are sometimes used off label but the evidence in primary insomnia is weak and anticholinergic effects and daytime sedation are common (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange an overnight polysomnogram before making any decision about treatment for him
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when there are features of apnoea, periodic limb movements or narcolepsy, and none is present with a normal airway and an Epworth score of 6 (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Start an antidepressant at a standard dose and review his sleep and mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Insomnia is frequently the presenting feature of depression, but he has no low mood, anhedonia or other depressive features on mental state examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder is diagnosed when difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep occurs at least three nights a week for at least three months with daytime consequences, despite adequate opportunity to sleep. It is maintained less by the original trigger than by the compensatory behaviours that follow, particularly spending longer in bed, napping and using the bed for wakeful activity, which weaken the association between bed and sleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia targets exactly these mechanisms through sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive work on catastrophic beliefs about sleep and relaxation training, and its benefit persists after treatment ends unlike that of hypnotics. Digital and group programs make it deliverable in Australian primary care, and hypnotics are best reserved for short courses in acute situational insomnia.
key_points: Three nights a week for three months with daytime impairment defines the disorder
Excessive time in bed, napping and working in bed perpetuate the problem
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its gains outlast treatment
Screen for depression, apnoea and restless legs before labelling insomnia primary
Hypnotics are for short term use in acute insomnia, not chronic disorder
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction therapy initially shortens time in bed to match actual sleep time with a floor of about five hours, and the transient increase in daytime sleepiness in the first fortnight is the reason patients must be warned before they drive.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing iron replacement before dopaminergic therapy in restless legs syndrome
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 39 year old woman who describes a crawling discomfort deep in both calves every evening. She says she has to get up and walk around to make it go away, that it is worst when she sits still after dinner, and that it settles completely while she is moving.

It has been present for a year and is now delaying her sleep by two hours most nights. She is a vegetarian with heavy periods. Her mood is normal, she takes no antidepressant or antipsychotic, and her renal function is normal. Neurological examination of the legs is normal with preserved reflexes, power and sensation, and there is no calf tenderness or swelling.

data_table.Examination: Normal lower limb power, tone, reflexes and sensation, no oedema or calf tenderness, no peripheral pulse deficit
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); ferritin 22 mcg/L (15-200); transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45); urea, electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low nightly dose and titrate it against her symptom response
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist is effective but risks augmentation with earlier and more intense symptoms over time, so it follows correction of iron status rather than preceding it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Begin oral iron replacement aiming for a ferritin above 75 mcg/L and reassess symptoms
options.rationale: Brain iron deficiency drives the syndrome and can exist with a ferritin that is technically within range, so replacement to a target well above the laboratory lower limit is the first intervention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Prescribe gabapentin at night and review both her sleep and her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: An alpha 2 delta ligand is a legitimate treatment particularly where pain is prominent, but it does not correct the iron deficiency that is the reversible driver here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Nerve conduction testing is for suspected peripheral neuropathy, which produces sensory loss or reflex change rather than a movement relieved urge with normal neurological examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night for four weeks and review her sleep pattern after that time
options.rationale: A hypnotic may shorten sleep latency but leaves the sensory urge untreated and risks dependence in a chronic condition (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis resting on an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensation, worse at rest, relieved by movement and worse in the evening or at night. Central nervous system iron deficiency is the best established mechanism, and peripheral ferritin correlates imperfectly with brain iron, which is why replacement is recommended when ferritin is below about 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation is below 20 per cent even though those values are within the standard laboratory range. Secondary causes worth excluding at the same visit include pregnancy, renal failure and drugs, particularly antidepressants, antipsychotics, lithium and sedating antihistamines. Dopamine agonists remain effective but carry the risk of augmentation, in which symptoms appear earlier in the day and spread to the arms, so alpha 2 delta ligands are increasingly preferred when drug treatment is needed.
key_points: Urge to move, worse at rest, relieved by movement, worse at night is the diagnostic tetrad
Replace iron if ferritin is below 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent
Review antidepressants, antipsychotics and sedating antihistamines as contributors
Dopamine agonists cause augmentation with long term use
Alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin are an alternative when drug therapy is needed
explanation.pearls: A ferritin of 22 mcg/L is reported as normal by most Australian laboratories but is well below the 75 mcg/L threshold used in restless legs syndrome, and treating to that higher target resolves symptoms in a substantial proportion without any dopaminergic drug.

subtopic_detail: Detecting and responding to disordered gambling presenting as an unexplained financial and mood crisis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 34 year old man presents asking for a mental health care plan for stress. He has taken out a second personal loan, has been borrowing from family with vague explanations, and has stopped seeing friends. He has lost 6 kg and sleeps four hours a night.

When you ask what the money went on, he becomes evasive, then says he has been using an online sports betting app since it was advertised during the football and that he has been chasing his losses for about a year. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He says he has thought that his family would be better off without him but has no plan and does not want to die.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, oriented with intact cognition, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start an antidepressant for his low mood and review both symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a role for comorbid depression but no established benefit for the gambling itself, and prescribing alone leaves the behaviour and the escalating debt untouched (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Arrange an urgent psychiatric admission because of the passive suicidal thoughts he described
options.rationale: Admission is warranted for intent, plan, means or an inability to stay safe, and passive thoughts without intent in an engaged patient are managed with a safety plan and rapid outpatient follow up (Source: RANZCP: Deliberate Self Harm).

options.text: Reassure him that the debt is the problem and refer him only to a financial counsellor
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a valuable component but treating the debt as the disorder ignores the behavioural condition that generated it and the suicide risk that accompanies it (Source: Gambling Help Online Australia).

options.text: Make a safety plan, refer for gambling specific psychological therapy, and discuss self exclusion
options.rationale: Disordered gambling carries a high suicide risk that must be addressed first, cognitive behavioural therapy is the treatment with the best evidence, and self exclusion from betting platforms removes access in the way that supports early abstinence (Source: Gambling Help Online Australia; RANZCP: Deliberate Self Harm).

options.text: Prescribe naltrexone at an anticraving dose and review his gambling behaviour in six weeks
options.rationale: Naltrexone has modest evidence in gambling disorder and is considered as an adjunct after psychological treatment has been organised rather than as an opening move (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is under detected in Australian primary care because patients rarely name it, presenting instead with stress, insomnia, relationship breakdown or unexplained debt. The features that identify it are preoccupation, escalating stakes, chasing losses, lying to conceal the extent of involvement and jeopardising relationships or employment, and the shift to online and in play sports betting has made concealment easier and losses faster. It carries one of the highest suicide rates of any behavioural condition, so risk assessment and a safety plan come first at the visit where it is disclosed. Treatment combines gambling specific cognitive behavioural therapy, financial counselling and practical access restriction through self exclusion registers and app blocking, with pharmacotherapy such as naltrexone considered as an adjunct.
key_points: Ask directly about gambling when debt, secrecy and social withdrawal appear together
Chasing losses and concealment are the two most useful screening features
Suicide risk is high and assessment precedes any other intervention
Cognitive behavioural therapy specific to gambling has the strongest evidence
Self exclusion and financial counselling are practical components of the plan
explanation.pearls: Australia has a national self exclusion register for online wagering that blocks a person from all licensed Australian betting services at once, and registering the patient at the consultation is often more effective than any single prescription.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a stressor linked disorder from major depression when function is preserved
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 51 year old woman was made redundant five weeks ago after 20 years with the same employer. Since then she has felt flat and tearful, worries about money and sleeps poorly in the first half of the night. She asks whether she should start an antidepressant.

She still walks the dog daily, enjoys her book club and laughed several times during the consultation when talking about her grandchildren. Her appetite and weight are unchanged, and she describes no diurnal variation in mood, early morning waking or psychomotor slowing. She denies thoughts of self harm, and neither she nor her family has ever been treated for a mood disorder. She scores 11 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9. She is applying for jobs and has an interview next week.

data_table.Examination: Tearful at times but reactive affect, normal speech rate, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 11 of 27; thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start sertraline at an antidepressant dose and review her symptoms again in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants show little benefit over placebo for stressor linked symptoms of this severity and commit her to months of treatment for a reaction that is likely to resolve as circumstances change (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy assessment given the severity of her low mood score
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is for severe, psychotic, catatonic or treatment resistant depression, none of which is present in a woman with reactive affect and preserved function (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam for her sleep and review the situation once she has found new work
options.rationale: A hypnotic addresses one symptom, risks dependence and offers nothing for the adjustment process that is driving the presentation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diagnose major depressive disorder and refer for psychological therapy plus an antidepressant
options.rationale: Preserved reactivity, intact pleasure in activities, unchanged appetite and no biological features argue against a major depressive episode despite the questionnaire score (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Offer structured psychological support with a mental health care plan and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Symptoms tied to an identifiable stressor with retained reactivity and function are best managed with psychological support and active review, which also detects the minority who progress to a depressive episode (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Adjustment disorder describes emotional or behavioural symptoms arising within three months of an identifiable stressor that are out of proportion to it or impair function, and it is distinguished from major depression by preserved mood reactivity, retained capacity for pleasure and the absence of the biological features of melancholia. Symptom questionnaires such as the Patient Health Questionnaire 9 quantify distress but do not make a diagnosis, and a moderate score in the setting of a recent loss should prompt a careful history rather than an automatic prescription. The evidence for antidepressants in adjustment disorder is weak, whereas psychological support, problem solving and practical assistance address the stressor itself. Active review matters because a minority do go on to meet criteria for a depressive episode, and the transition is easily missed if the patient is discharged after a single visit.
key_points: Adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor within three months
Preserved reactivity and retained pleasure argue against major depression
Questionnaire scores measure severity but do not establish the diagnosis
Antidepressants have weak evidence in stressor linked presentations
Scheduled review detects the minority who progress to a depressive episode
explanation.pearls: Anhedonia that persists even in the patient's favourite activity is a far better discriminator of major depression than any questionnaire score, because a person with adjustment disorder still brightens when the subject changes.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy decision for nicotine dependence acquired through vaping in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 16 year old girl attends alone and asks for help stopping vaping. She has used a disposable nicotine vape daily for 18 months, now vapes within ten minutes of waking, and gets headaches and irritability by mid morning at school if she does not use it.

She has tried to stop three times, the longest for two days. She has never smoked cigarettes. She has no psychiatric history, no low mood or suicidal thoughts, takes no medication and is not pregnant. You have assessed her as a mature minor who understands the treatment being discussed. She scores 7 on a nicotine dependence questionnaire.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiorespiratory examination, normal mental state examination, no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; no other investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer behavioural support with nicotine replacement therapy and arrange structured follow up
options.rationale: Withdrawal within an hour of waking indicates significant dependence, and combining behavioural support with nicotine replacement is the recommended approach for a dependent adolescent (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start varenicline at the standard adult dose and review her tolerance of it in two weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is effective in adults but is not established in people under 18, so it is not the first choice in an adolescent who has not tried replacement therapy (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation with behavioural support alone and review her progress in four weeks
options.rationale: Behavioural support alone suits low dependence, but three failed attempts with early morning use and withdrawal symptoms indicate she needs pharmacological help as well (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation).

options.text: Recommend switching to a lower nicotine concentration vape and gradually reducing over time
options.rationale: Continued vaping maintains dependence and product nicotine labelling is unreliable, so this substitutes an unregulated device for a therapeutic one with measured dosing (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation).

options.text: Start bupropion at a cessation dose and review both her mood and her cravings in two weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is second line even in adults, lowers the seizure threshold and is not recommended for adolescents (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Adolescent nicotine dependence acquired through vaping is now a routine presentation in Australian general practice, and the products involved often deliver nicotine salts at concentrations well above those of a cigarette, producing rapid and severe dependence. Time to first use after waking is the most practical bedside measure of dependence, and use within 30 minutes indicates that behavioural support alone is unlikely to succeed. Nicotine replacement therapy is the pharmacotherapy with the best safety data in young people, and combination therapy pairing a patch for background craving with a short acting form for breakthrough urges outperforms either alone. Varenicline and bupropion are not established below the age of 18, and continuing to vape at a lower stated concentration is unreliable because labelled nicotine content frequently does not match the actual content.
key_points: Time to first use after waking is the most useful measure of nicotine dependence
Nicotine replacement therapy is the preferred pharmacotherapy in adolescents
Combination patch plus short acting replacement beats either alone
Varenicline and bupropion are not established under 18 years of age
Labelled nicotine concentration on vaping products is often inaccurate
explanation.pearls: A patient who vapes within 30 minutes of waking has dependence severe enough that behavioural support alone rarely succeeds, and that single question is more informative than the number of puffs or pods per day.

subtopic_detail: Separating persistent bereavement related distress from a depressive episode more than a year after a death
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a consultation clinic. A 62 year old woman was referred 15 months after her husband died suddenly. She thinks about him for most of the day, keeps his clothes laid out and his phone charged, and cannot bring herself to enter their bedroom. She says she feels that part of her died with him and that she has no idea who she is now.

She has stopped seeing the friends they had together because being with couples is unbearable, and she has not returned to the volunteering she loved. She eats and sleeps reasonably and her weight is unchanged. She feels intense yearning that comes in waves triggered by reminders rather than a constant flat mood, and she still laughs with her granddaughter. Her guilt centres on things she wishes she had said to him rather than on her own worthlessness, and she denies psychomotor slowing or thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect with tearfulness on discussing her husband, normal speech and psychomotor activity, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night and review her sleep, appetite and mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine targets the appetite and sleep disturbance of a depressive episode, and both are preserved here while the core problem is persistent yearning and identity disruption (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychotherapy addressing avoidance and restoration of daily roles
options.rationale: Yearning and preoccupation persisting beyond 12 months with identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and role withdrawal define prolonged grief disorder, and targeted psychotherapy is the treatment with the best evidence (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders; BMJ Best Practice: Grief).

options.text: Reassure her that grief has no timetable and review her again in six months if needed
options.rationale: Normalising is right for uncomplicated grief, but symptoms persisting beyond a year with functional withdrawal identify a treatable disorder rather than an expected trajectory (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Start an antidepressant with a mood stabiliser and review her response again in six weeks
options.rationale: Combination pharmacotherapy is for treatment resistant or bipolar depression and is unjustified in a woman with no depressive episode and no history of elevated mood (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Arrange cognitive testing and neuroimaging to investigate her sense of altered identity
options.rationale: The altered sense of self here is the identity disruption characteristic of persistent grief, not a cognitive deficit, and her cognition is intact on examination (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder entered the main diagnostic classifications recently and describes intense yearning or preoccupation with a deceased person persisting for at least 12 months in adults, accompanied by features such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, intense loneliness and difficulty re engaging with life. It is separated from a major depressive episode by the object of the distress, since grief comes in waves triggered by reminders with preserved capacity for pleasure elsewhere, whereas depression produces pervasive low mood, guilt about the self, anhedonia across domains and biological disturbance. The distinction is practical rather than academic because antidepressants have not shown benefit for the grief symptoms themselves, whereas structured grief focused psychotherapy targeting avoidance and restoration of roles does. The two can coexist, so a depressive episode should be actively screened for and treated on its own merits if present.
key_points: The 12 month threshold in adults distinguishes prolonged grief disorder from acute grief
Identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and role withdrawal are core features
Grief comes in waves with preserved reactivity whereas depression is pervasive
Guilt in grief concerns the deceased whereas depressive guilt concerns the self
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for the grief symptoms
explanation.pearls: Keeping a deceased partner's possessions untouched while avoiding the room they are in is the combination of holding on and avoidance that distinguishes prolonged grief disorder, and both behaviours are direct targets of grief focused psychotherapy.

subtopic_detail: Excessive daytime sleepiness with emotionally triggered weakness misattributed to a mood disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar. A 19 year old university student is referred with two years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness that a previous doctor treated as depression, without benefit from two adequate antidepressant trials.

He falls asleep in lectures and once at the dinner table, and says a 15 minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours. When he laughs hard at a joke his knees buckle and his jaw sags for a few seconds while he stays fully aware of what is happening. On waking he sometimes cannot move for half a minute and has seen figures at the end of his bed while otherwise awake. His mood is reactive, he enjoys his sport and friends, and he denies anhedonia, guilt or suicidal thoughts. His body mass index is 23 kg/m2, he does not snore and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 19.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, Mallampati class 1 airway, reactive affect with no depressive cognitions
data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 of 24; full blood count, iron studies and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and review his energy in six weeks
options.rationale: A third antidepressant continues to treat a depressive episode that is not present, given reactive mood, preserved enjoyment and absent depressive cognitions (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Prescribe modafinil for daytime sleepiness and review his alertness again in four weeks
options.rationale: Wake promoting therapy is a mainstay of treatment but is started after the diagnosis is confirmed, since prior stimulant exposure confounds the sleep latency testing (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day
options.rationale: Sleepiness with refreshing naps, emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with retained awareness, sleep paralysis and hypnopompic hallucinations point to narcolepsy, and overnight study followed by daytime latency testing is the diagnostic pathway (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to investigate the episodes of collapse he describes
options.rationale: Electroencephalography investigates atonic seizures, whose near pair feature is impaired awareness during the attack, whereas he remains fully aware throughout (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry at home and start positive airway pressure if it is abnormal
options.rationale: Home oximetry screens for sleep disordered breathing, which is unlikely with a normal body mass index, no snoring and an unobstructed airway (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurones and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, which is exactly when depression is also common, so misdiagnosis is frequent and the average delay to correct diagnosis runs to years. The pentad is excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep, and cataplexy is close to specific when it involves brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with fully preserved awareness. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of sleep disruption, followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day showing a short mean sleep latency with at least two episodes of rapid eye movement sleep occurring soon after sleep onset. Antidepressants must usually be withdrawn before the study because they suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can mask the diagnostic pattern.
key_points: Refreshing short naps distinguish narcolepsy from the unrefreshing sleepiness of depression
Cataplexy is emotionally triggered brief atonia with fully preserved awareness
Diagnosis is polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day
Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and confound the latency test
Sleep paralysis and hypnopompic hallucinations complete the clinical picture
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants and stimulants generally need to be withdrawn about two weeks before a multiple sleep latency test, because rapid eye movement suppression can convert a diagnostic study into a normal one.

subtopic_detail: Mood and behavioural change from androgen misuse presenting as a primary psychiatric disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old man brought by his partner because of four months of irritability, verbal aggression and jealous accusations. He has been sleeping five hours a night, feels unusually confident and has been training at the gym twice a day.

He has gained 9 kg of muscle in that time, has acne across his back and shoulders, and his partner has noticed tender swelling under both nipples. He denies grandiose delusions and there are no hallucinations or thought disorder. He drinks little and uses no illicit stimulants, and a urine drug screen for amphetamines, cocaine and cannabis is negative. There is no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. When asked specifically what he takes for training, he says only protein powder and a testosterone booster from an overseas website.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Marked muscle bulk, truncal acne, bilateral tender gynaecomastia, small testes, no tremor or hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines, cocaine and cannabis; haematocrit 0.54 (0.40-0.52); alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40); high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.7 mmol/L (greater than 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start olanzapine for the irritability and arrange psychiatric review again in two weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic treats the surface symptom while the driving exposure continues, and it adds metabolic harm to an already adverse lipid and cardiovascular profile (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start lithium for a first manic episode and arrange monitoring of his serum concentrations
options.rationale: A first manic episode is the near diagnosis here, but the absence of any family or personal history alongside physical signs of androgen excess points to a substance induced picture (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer for couples counselling to address the jealousy and review his mood in six weeks
options.rationale: Relationship work may help later, but attributing the change to interpersonal conflict misses a reversible physical cause with cardiovascular and hepatic consequences (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Take a targeted history of injectable androgen use and measure testosterone and gonadotrophins
options.rationale: Rapid muscle gain, acne, gynaecomastia, small testes, hypertension, raised haematocrit and suppressed high density lipoprotein indicate exogenous androgen use, and suppressed gonadotrophins with a high testosterone confirm it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Admit him involuntarily under the mental health act for assessment of his aggression
options.rationale: Involuntary assessment requires risk that cannot be managed voluntarily, and he is engaging with the consultation without threat or intent to harm (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Androgenic anabolic steroid use is common among young men training intensively and is rarely volunteered, because products bought online are described as supplements or boosters rather than as injectable hormones. The psychiatric presentation of irritability, aggression, reduced sleep need and grandiosity closely mimics a manic or mixed episode, and the discriminating information is physical rather than psychological: rapid lean mass gain, truncal acne, gynaecomastia from peripheral aromatisation, testicular atrophy, hypertension, polycythaemia, transaminase rise and suppressed high density lipoprotein cholesterol. Biochemically the picture is a high or supraphysiological testosterone with suppressed luteinising and follicle stimulating hormone, the reverse of the pattern seen in genuine hypogonadism. Management is cessation with support for the withdrawal depression that follows, monitoring of haematocrit, lipids and liver enzymes, and endocrine follow up because recovery of the gonadal axis can take many months.
key_points: Ask specifically about injectable androgens rather than about drugs in general
Gynaecomastia, acne, small testes and rapid muscle gain are the physical clues
High testosterone with suppressed gonadotrophins confirms an exogenous source
Polycythaemia, hypertension and low high density lipoprotein drive cardiovascular risk
Withdrawal depression after cessation carries a real suicide risk and needs follow up
explanation.pearls: A haematocrit above 0.54 in an androgen user is an indication for cessation and venesection, since the resulting hyperviscosity contributes directly to the strokes and myocardial infarctions seen in this group.
